messages.content:
Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Generator scaffolding left in: oaicite, [cite: 1], placeholders -- finish the text and read it
- The "it's not X, it's Y" construction -- just state Y
- A bolded word opening a list item as a per-item tag -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- Saying "is" the long way: serves as, boasts, functions as -- use the plain verb
- One-line dramatic fragments: "That's it. That's the whole thing." -- cut them, the preceding sentence already made the point
- Em dashes clustering in one document -- most drafts need 0-2; use commas, periods or parentheses for the rest
- Filler verbs: leverages, facilitates, unlocks -- use a plain verb, or cut the sentence
- A snake_case identifier written as plain prose -- name it in words, or mark it as inline code
- Marketing cliches: "hidden gem", "let's dive in" -- say the specific thing
- The "Not X. Not Y." listing construction -- state the point once
- Stock section skeleton: "Despite its success", "Looking ahead" -- name the specific thing the section is for
- Standalone filler adverbs: undoubtedly, arguably, notably, importantly, ultimately -- most add nothing; cut them unless one is carrying real emphasis
- A banned synonym of one of this project's canonical terms, per its declared lexicon -- one word, one meaning: use the canonical term the word's own note names
- Dramatic turning points with nothing concrete behind them: "Everything changed." -- name the actual event, or cut it

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a post about why a company is investing in developer relations. Around 250 words.

output:
We're hiring a developer relations team this quarter, and I want to explain the reasoning rather than announce it.

Last year we shipped an API that we thought was self-explanatory. Our docs covered every endpoint. Support tickets said otherwise: 40% of them were people who had read the docs and still built the wrong thing. The docs described what each call did. Nobody had written down how the calls fit together for the three or four jobs people actually came to us for.

That gap is the work. Developer relations, done well, means someone whose job is to build with our product the way a customer would, hit the same walls, and then either fix the wall or write the guide that gets people past it. That person has to be senior enough to file a pull request against the SDK, not just a bug report about it.

The other half is upstream. Our roadmap is currently shaped by whoever escalates loudest through sales. Developers who churn quietly at the integration stage never show up in that signal. We want a team that sits in the Discord, reads the GitHub issues nobody triaged, and brings the pattern back to engineering with enough detail to act on.

We're measuring this on time-to-first-successful-call and on integration-stage churn, not on conference talks or follower counts. If those two numbers don't move in twelve months, the approach was wrong and we'll say so.

Two roles are open now: one engineer-facing, one docs-and-education. Both report into engineering, not marketing. That placement is deliberate.
